messages.content:
You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The input describes a hexagonal crystal with lattice parameters a = b = 5.79109938 Å, c = 11.854699 Å, α = β = 90.0°, and γ = 119.99999292° (essentially 120°, with a minute deviation of about 7.08 × 10⁻⁶ degrees from the ideal hexagonal angle). The input cell contains 20 atoms with composition Nb₆Ni₂S₁₂, corresponding to six niobium, two nickel, and twelve sulfur atoms. The structure is described in space group P6₃22 (number 182, Hall symbol P 6c 2c), a chiral hexagonal space group with sixfold screw symmetry along the c-axis.

The relationship between the input and standard crystallographic frames is given by q_standard = P q_input + s, where the transformation matrix P is effectively the identity matrix with negligible off-diagonal terms on the order of 10⁻¹⁷ or smaller, and the origin shift s is (0.9999989999999999, 0.9999989999999999, 0.0). This means the input and standard frames are coincident to within about 10⁻⁶ fractional units in the a and b directions, with no shift along c, and the input cell is essentially the conventional hexagonal cell.

The atomic structure is built from four independent crystallographic orbits. Niobium occupies two distinct sites: the 2a Wyckoff position at (0, 0, 0) with multiplicity two, placing Nb atoms at the origin and related by symmetry; and the 4f position at (1/3, 2/3, z) with z = 0.503113, multiplicity four, forming a second niobium sublattice displaced along the threefold axis. Nickel occupies the 2c position at (1/3, 2/3, 1/4), also with multiplicity two, situated on the same threefold axis as the 4f niobium but at a different height. Sulfur occupies the general 12i position at (x, y, z) = (0.000863, 0.332689, 0.132452), with multiplicity twelve, generating the full sulfur sublattice through the space group symmetry operations.

The input coordinates were recorded to six decimal places, and small precision corrections were applied to account for rounding in the original data. For the niobium 2a site, the input listed positions at (0.000001, 0.000001, 0.0) and (0.000001, 0.000001, 0.5), which were corrected by displacements of (−0.000001, −0.000001, 0.0) to bring them to the exact special position (0, 0, 0) and its symmetry equivalent. The four niobium 4f atoms were input at (0.333334, 0.666668, 0.503113), (0.666668, 0.333334, 0.003113), (0.666668, 0.333334, 0.496887), and (0.333334, 0.666668, 0.996887), each corrected by approximately (−0.000001, −0.000001, 0.0) to align with the ideal 1/3 and 2/3 fractional coordinates. Similarly, the two nickel atoms at (0.333334, 0.666668, 0.25) and (0.666668, 0.333334, 0.75) received the same small corrections to their x and y coordinates.

The twelve sulfur atoms, being in a general position, required individual corrections. The representative sulfur at (0.000864, 0.332690, 0.132452) was displaced by (−0.000002, −0.000002, 0.0). Other sulfur atoms at positions such as (0.667312, 0.668175, 0.132452), (0.332690, 0.331827, 0.632452), (0.668175, 0.000864, 0.632452), (0.332690, 0.000864, 0.867548), (0.668175, 0.667312, 0.867548), (0.331827, 0.332690, 0.367548), and (0.000864, 0.668175, 0.367548) each received corrections on the order of 10⁻⁶ fractional units in x and/or y, with no adjustment to their z coordinates. These corrections reflect the rounding precision of the input data rather than any deviation from the ideal space group symmetry, and they preserve the real input geometry while refining the coordinates to be consistent with the crystallographic symmetry operations.

The overall structure thus consists of niobium atoms distributed over two sublattices—one at the cell origin and one along the threefold axis at approximately half the c-axis height—nickel atoms at one-quarter and three-quarters along the threefold axis, and a twelvefold sulfur sublattice filling the general positions, all arranged within the hexagonal P6₃22 symmetry framework.
